items.source: John Authers (Bloomberg Opinion) via Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: 5% Treasury yields aren't a crisis — they're 40 years of history reasserting itself
items.idea: The 10yr UST is near 20-year highs but still below the average that prevailed through nearly all of 1965-2007. Term premium (Bloomberg Economics) has been flat over the past year even as yields rose, and per Apollo's Torsten Slok, the US term premium is still below Germany's and Japan's — undercutting the 'America is losing bond-market credibility' narrative.
items.angle: The bear case for equities isn't 5% yields per se — it's the combination of a sudden re-rate AND an earnings miss. As long as the AI capex bet keeps paying off, valuation compression (23x→19.4x fwd P/E already priced) can absorb it quietly.
items.tweetA: Everyone's staring at the 10yr near cycle highs like it's a warning light. Nobody's asking why German and Japanese term premia are HIGHER than ours. The bond market isn't panicking about US credibility — it's just re-pricing 6 fewer Fed cuts than expected in January.
items.tweetB: Fwd P/E on the S&P went from 23x to 19.4x since October and nobody noticed because earnings kept the index flat. That's the 'invisible' bear market — multiple compression hiding behind EPS growth. Watch what happens the day AI capex ROI gets questioned.

charts.desc: 🔥 Multiple embedded Bloomberg charts: 10yr yield vs 40yr history (the standout), Atlanta Fed Wagetracker, US term premium (Bloomberg Economics), EM FX index, forward P/E vs bond yield.

items.source: John Authers (Bloomberg Opinion) via Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Fed's rate decision is a literal coin toss — Warsh vs Waller read the same data oppositely
items.idea: Warsh went hawkish at Jackson Hole after an unconvincing July hold; last week's stronger-than-expected August jobs report added hawkish weight. Waller counters that 3-month core CPI fell from 4.76% (Feb) to 3.05% (July) — a steady disinflation trend that argues for patience. Friday's CPI is the tiebreaker before the Sep 15-16 FOMC.
items.angle: This is a genuine coin-flip meeting, which options markets should be pricing as elevated realized-vol risk into FOMC, not a formality.
items.tweetA: Two Fed officials, same data, opposite conclusions. Warsh sees August jobs and gets hawkish. Waller sees core CPI cut in half since February and gets patient. Friday's CPI print isn't just an economic release — it's the actual FOMC vote.
items.tweetB: Core CPI 4.76% in Feb, 3.05% in July — one of the fastest disinflation runs of this cycle, and the market still can't decide if the Fed hikes next week. If Waller's framing wins, this is a buy-the-dip setup on rate-sensitives into September.

charts.desc: Atlanta Fed Wagetracker chart and August employment surprise chart embedded.

items.source: John Authers (Bloomberg Opinion) via Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: EM currencies just broke the old 'higher US rates = stronger dollar' playbook
items.idea: The MSCI EM Currency Index has risen for 11 straight weeks — its longest streak since 2007 — even as Bloomberg Economics' gauge of Fed sentiment turns more hawkish. Local-currency EM bonds returned +3.6% YTD vs -0.6% for US Treasuries. JPMorgan's Bareau now frames EM as an 'income diversifier,' not just a high-beta growth bet.
items.angle: Rate differentials are being crowded out by better EM balance sheets, high real yields and commodity terms of trade — worth testing whether this decoupling survives a hawkish September FOMC surprise or was just a low-vol summer artifact.
items.tweetA: MSCI EM currencies just logged their longest win streak since 2007 — while the Fed is getting MORE hawkish, not less. The old dollar-smile trade is broken, and nobody's repriced EM local debt for it yet.
items.tweetB: EM local bonds: +3.6% YTD. US Treasuries: -0.6%. That's not a rounding error, that's a full regime flip in who gets paid to hold duration. The 'buy US, sell EM on higher rates' playbook just stopped working.

items.source: John Authers (Bloomberg Opinion) via Dark Side of the Boom
items.title: Petrobras + Grupo Mexico = 40% of LatAm's entire equity return this year
items.idea: Morningstar's Madeleine Black attributes ~40% of Latin America's YTD equity return through August to just two stocks — Petrobras (oil) and Grupo Mexico (copper) — as the Middle East conflict and the AI-driven copper squeeze collide. LatAm equity ETFs pulled in a record $3.6B in 7 months, nearly double all of 2025's $1.8B. Strip out Taiwan/Korea semis and BCA's Budaghyan finds broad EM hasn't actually outperformed.
items.angle: The 'EM rally' headline is really two commodity stocks plus two chip exporters — a much narrower, more fragile story than the index-level narrative suggests, and one that lives or dies with oil and copper prices specifically.
items.tweetA: Two stocks — Petrobras and Grupo Mexico — are 40% of Latin America's entire equity return this year. That's not a regional rally, that's a leveraged bet on oil and copper wearing an EM index costume.
items.tweetB: Strip out Taiwan and Korea's chipmakers and EM equities haven't actually broken out at all, per BCA. The 'AI beneficiary' rotation is real — it's just concentrated in about four stocks across two continents, not a broad EM story.

items.title: MacroEdge: oil/gas beats AI as the Q4 trade — 5-7mmbpd of Middle East flow still offline
items.idea: Author argues oil and gas, not AI/semis, is the most important trade of Q4 2026, citing persistent Middle East supply disruption of 5-7mmbpd, escalating Ansarallah-Saudi tensions, and a simultaneous copper melt-up plus sharp 3-month wheat rally as evidence of a genuine commodity inflation impulse — drawing technical parallels to late 2021 and late 2007.
items.angle: A direct rebuttal to the 'AI capex is the only story' consensus — worth triangulating against Goldman's Brent target hike and the copper/nickel break below for a combined commodity-inflation thesis into CPI week.
items.tweetA: A macro strategist is telling clients oil & gas beats AI/semis into Q4. Not despite 5-7mmbpd of Middle East supply still offline — because of it. When was the last time you heard someone say that out loud?
items.tweetB: Copper record high. Wheat up sharply in 3 months. 5-7mmbpd of oil flow still disrupted. That's not one commodity story, it's three converging at once — and Friday's CPI print is about to tell us if the Fed is already behind it.

charts.desc: Copper melt-up chart and softs (wheat) 3-month price chart embedded in report.

items.title: '$4M is the new $1M' — and your spending peaks in your 30s, not your 60s
items.idea: Argues net-worth targets are structurally miscalibrated: lifestyle-improvement value flattens hard after a paid-off home plus $3-5M liquid (~$120-200k/yr spend). Real spending peaks in your 30s (business-building + house + young kids), not retirement — most self-employed people 'overshoot' their true FI number because earned income ends up running 4-5x investment income once a business scales.
items.angle: A client-conversation grenade: the standard '$X by 65' wealth-planning framework may be structurally wrong for anyone running their own business — worth testing against actual client withdrawal and spending-curve data.
items.tweetA: Your financial plan probably has your net worth peaking at 65. Your actual spending peaked at 35. Nobody builds a plan around that mismatch, but it's the real reason people die with more money than they ever needed.
items.tweetB: 'Escape velocity' at 35-45, not 65 — the framing isn't hustle culture, it's math: once a business scales, earned income runs 4-5x investment income, and you can't spend that fast even trying. Retirement planning has this exactly backwards.

items.title: CXMT hit 10% global DRAM share in one year — and just landed Xiaomi's flagship phone
items.idea: Counterpoint Research: CXMT's global DRAM share went from 4% to 10% year-over-year in Q2 — a threshold analysts didn't expect for another year. Xiaomi's next flagship will ship on CXMT mobile memory, its first major commercial win against Samsung/SK Hynix in a flagship phone. Goldman estimates CXMT could supply 50% of China's DRAM demand and 40% of its HBM demand by 2028, making it the de facto fourth HBM supplier behind the trillion-dollar three (Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron).
items.angle: Apple is reportedly testing CXMT memory for iPhone/MacBook amid a ~38% BOM increase from the memory shortage alone — watch for a political 'blessing' around the Sep 24 Xi-Trump meeting. Direct read-through to $MU pricing power if the entity-list wall cracks.
items.tweetA: CXMT went from 4% to 10% of global DRAM in twelve months and Xiaomi just put it in a flagship phone. Everyone's watching Nvidia's China chip fight. The real chokepoint battle is memory, and China just won a round nobody priced in.
items.tweetB: Micron just pledged $250B in US investment and is lobbying DC to keep CXMT off the entity list. That's not confidence, that's a company that knows what happens to its 75% margins if Apple gets the green light to dual-source out of China. $MU

charts.desc: No embedded chart in this email — WSJ source article on CXMT's investor day likely has a share-growth chart. Charts inside — worth opening.

items.title: Memory now eats up to 40% of a flagship phone's BOM — Tim Cook's '100-year flood'
items.idea: iPhone 18 Pro's bill-of-materials rose ~38% from memory pricing alone; memory's share of a flagship's parts cost has gone from ~10% to 33-40% in about two years. Apple has already raised Mac, iPad and iPhone prices 15-25% in response. Cook called it a '100-year flood' in memory pricing on the July earnings call.
items.angle: A hard input-cost data point for anyone modeling consumer-electronics margins into 2026-27 — memory scarcity is now a bigger swing factor for phone/PC OEM margins than tariffs.
items.tweetA: Memory went from 10% to 40% of a flagship phone's cost in about two years. That's not a supply chain hiccup, that's a structural repricing of the single most important input in every device with a chip. $AAPL passed it straight to consumers — 15-25% price hikes across the lineup.
items.tweetB: Tim Cook calling memory a '100-year flood' on an earnings call is corporate-speak for 'we have no leverage.' Apple's whole supply chain moat — the thing that made it tech's most resilient OEM — doesn't work when the shortage is upstream of everyone.

items.title: Drones aren't replacing tanks — they're changing what a tank costs to keep alive
items.idea: Deutsche Bank Research frames Ukraine and the Middle East as proof that cheap, AI-enabled drones impose disproportionate costs on expensive conventional assets, projecting the global military-drone market to grow ~8%/yr through 2030 (Europe ~13%). Ukraine has pivoted from wartime necessity to an export/manufacturing power, with production links spreading into Europe and the Gulf. The catch: drone supply chains (magnets, graphite, gallium, germanium) remain deeply China-dependent.
items.angle: The investable surface is wider than a single 'drone stock' — modular manufacturing, sensors, counter-drone systems and maintenance are where DB thinks the money actually is, and it's all gated by the same critical-minerals chokepoint China controls in the EV and chip stories too.
items.tweetA: Europe's military drone market growing 13%/year through 2030 and the bottleneck isn't manufacturing capacity — it's magnets, gallium and germanium, still mostly Chinese. The West is trying to re-arm with a supply chain it doesn't control.
items.tweetB: Ukraine went from 'country under siege' to drone exporter to the Gulf and Europe in about three years. That's the actual defense-tech story of the decade, and it's happening through commercial-style manufacturing scale-up, not defense primes.

charts.desc: Charts inside — worth opening the full Deutsche Bank research note for market-size projections.

items.title: Bitcoin 'chopsolidating' below the 50-week MA after a 30%+ rally off mid-$60ks
items.idea: After rallying 30%+ off the mid-$60k region, BTC is consolidating just below what the author calls the 'Bears Last Stand' level near the 50-week MA, with a moderate uptick in profit-taking from BOTH short-term AND long-term holder cohorts — a nuance the author flags as worth distinguishing (full on-chain analysis paywalled).
items.angle: Dual-cohort profit-taking (not just STH, which is normal, but LTH too) is typically a late-rally caution signal on-chain — worth cross-checking against the debasement-trade framing elsewhere in this window for whether BTC's rally still has a macro tailwind or is running out of on-chain fuel.
items.tweetA: Both short-term AND long-term BTC holders are taking profit right now. STH selling into strength is normal. LTH selling alongside them is the tell that usually shows up near local tops, not mid-rally.
items.tweetB: BTC is +30% off the mid-$60ks and stalling right at the 'Bears Last Stand' level on the weekly chart. Round-number psychology aside, this is exactly where a real breakout separates itself from a failed retest.

items.title: Goldman hikes Brent target to $85 for Dec-2026 — but spot at $97 says the market doesn't believe it
items.idea: Goldman raised its Dec-2026 Brent/WTI forecasts by $5 to $85/$80, and its 2027 averages to $80/$75 — yet Brent spot trades around $97, a ~$12 premium to Goldman's own 15-month-out target. Goldman calls the move measured because Gulf supply adaptation (pipelines, alternative shipping, opaque flows) has offset the disruption more than expected, but flags that a sustained Gulf export shortfall could push Brent above $120/bbl.
items.angle: That $97 spot vs $85 forecast gap IS the trade — either the market is pricing tail risk Goldman's base case ignores, or Goldman's revision is a lagging indicator and spot rolls over hard once the Hormuz workaround gets tested. Worth pairing directly against MacroEdge's oil/gas-over-AI Q4 call.
items.tweetA: Goldman raises its 2026 Brent target to $85. Oil is trading at $97. That's not a rounding error, that's the market pricing in a real chance the Gulf workaround fails that Goldman's own base case doesn't. Someone's wrong here.
items.tweetB: $85 base case, $120+ tail risk, $97 spot sitting almost exactly between the two. Crude right now is basically a referendum on whether 'the market learned to trade around Hormuz' or just got lucky for a few months. $USO $XLE

items.title: A 175-year-old nickel-copper pricing rule is breaking in real time
items.idea: Nickel has carried a price premium to copper for over a century; that spread is now closing fast as copper sets fresh all-time highs on AI/grid/EV electrification demand while Indonesia-driven nickel supply keeps growing. Independently flagged the same day by Bloomberg Opinion's David Fickling ('A 175-Year Commodity Market Rule Is Starting to Break').
items.angle: When two independent commodity desks flag the same century-old relationship breaking in the same 24 hours, the move is usually already well underway, not a contrarian call — copper's structural AI-driven demand story now has its own historical anomaly attached as a talking point.
items.tweetA: Nickel has been worth more than copper for 175 years. That's over. Copper's AI/grid demand broke a relationship older than the modern periodic table. Two different desks flagged this the same day — that's not coincidence, that's confirmation.
items.tweetB: Everyone's pricing copper off 'AI needs wire.' The more interesting chart is nickel — Indonesia flooded supply while nobody was watching, and a 175-year premium just evaporated. The AI trade broke a commodity relationship it wasn't even trying to touch.

charts.desc: 🔥 The copper-vs-nickel 175-year spread chart is the single best chart of this window — a genuine 'never seen before' relationship break, simple and visual enough to tweet standalone.

items.title: Fed model says funds rate 'should' be 5% right now — that's 125bps behind the curve
items.idea: Topdown Charts' model (inflation expectations + labor market) implies the fed funds rate should be ~5% vs the actual 3.75% — a 125bp gap. Inflation expectations have re-anchored higher, the labor market is tightening again, and over 40% of global central banks have already pivoted into hike mode. Author calls a September hike near-certain and flags a classic contrarian bearish setup: US equities at record valuation/allocation/sentiment extremes could turn a hike into a 'spark to powder.'
items.angle: The most explicit 'the Fed is behind, not ahead' framework in this window — pairs directly with the Warsh/Waller coin-toss item above. If Thomas is right about September/October seasonal correction risk, that's the setup, with a year-end seasonal rally as the second-order trade to have on the shelf.
items.tweetA: A model just said the Fed funds rate should be 5%, not 3.75%. That's not a rounding error, that's 125bps of 'behind the curve' hiding in plain sight while everyone debates whether September is even a hike month.
items.tweetB: Record valuations, record allocations, record sentiment — and a Fed that's arguably still 125bps too loose. That's not a soft landing setup, that's dry powder waiting for a spark. September/October seasonality just became the spark's most likely delivery date.

charts.desc: 🔥 The fed-funds-model 'implied rate' chart is the standout — shows the ~125bp gap between modeled and actual policy rate directly, plus two supporting charts on inflation expectations and labor-market tightness.

items.title: The optics fight nobody's watching: MOPA vs single-cavity lasers for AI datacenter interconnects
items.idea: For co-packaged optics (CPO/NPO) — the laser light sources feeding AI datacenter interconnects — two architectures are competing: Lumentum's single-cavity ultra-high-power laser vs. a MOPA (Master Oscillator Power Amplifier) approach that boosts a low-power seed laser ~4x (6dB) via a semiconductor optical amplifier, championed by Sumitomo and Nanjing University research. MOPA is easier to yield at the seed-laser stage but pushes the hard engineering problem into amplifier design and integration.
items.angle: A genuine 'which vendor wins the socket' question for the optics layer of AI infrastructure — a much less crowded trade than GPUs/HBM, and the answer determines who captures margin in CPO as hyperscalers move optics on-package to cut power and heat in AI racks.
items.tweetA: Everyone's arguing about GPUs and HBM. There's a quieter fight happening in the laser that has to sit next to every AI accelerator doing co-packaged optics — Lumentum's single-cavity design vs a MOPA challenger from Sumitomo. Whoever wins owns a socket nobody's pricing in yet.
items.tweetB: MOPA lasers push the hard problem from 'build a stable high-power cavity' to 'build an amplifier that doesn't degrade signal quality at high gain.' Same problem, different place to hide it. Worth knowing before someone tells you CPO optics are a solved problem.

charts.desc: Architecture diagram of MOPA laser (seed + SOA amplifier, via Coherent) — technical, not tweet-alone material, but clarifies the whole thesis.
